Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Vignette:
# Talia's Testimony

Talia was sixty-six when she walked into the clinic on a Tuesday morning, her hands trembling slightly as she filled out the intake form. She had owned her small fabric and yarn shop on the main street of her town for nearly thirty years—a business built from nothing after her divorce, a source of pride and identity that had anchored her through decades of steady, unspectacular life. She was Samoan, first-generation American, raised to be self-reliant and to keep difficulties private. That she was here at all meant something had finally broken through her own resistance.

The event that brought her to this threshold had occurred two years earlier, on an evening in late March at approximately 7:15 p.m. Talia had been closing the shop, counting the till and tidying the front display, when three police officers entered without announcement. What followed was a confrontation that Talia still struggled to articulate—there had been a report, a mistake, something about merchandise allegedly stolen from another business. She remembered the officers' voices, their physical proximity, the way one of them had grabbed her arm when she reached toward her phone. She remembered being pushed against the counter, her glasses falling, the sensation of her own helplessness. The details fragmented there. She could not recall how long it lasted, could not reconstruct the exact sequence of what happened after the initial contact, could not fully explain why the officers had finally left or what words had been exchanged at the end. The memory felt like a film with missing frames—visceral in its emotional weight but impossible to narrate as a coherent sequence.

What remained undeniable was the aftermath. Within weeks, Talia had begun to avoid closing the shop alone. She hired her niece to work evenings, an expense she could not really afford. More broadly, she began to avoid the darkness—she installed motion-sensor lights throughout the shop and her home, kept every room illuminated after sunset. She stopped going out in the early evening, the hour when the event had occurred. At 7:15 p.m., she would feel her chest tighten, her breathing shallow, a sense of dread that had no manageable proportions. She came to believe that something in her had broken, that her inability to fight back or to even clearly remember what had happened proved she was inadequate, that she lacked whatever internal resources allowed other people to endure trauma and remain intact.

The feeling of being watched had become pervasive. In her own shop, while customers browsed the shelves, Talia would experience sudden vertigo—a sensation that the room was tilting, that she could not trust her own equilibrium. She interpreted these moments as evidence that she was losing her grip on reality, that her mind was fragmenting in response to what had happened. She had come to believe that normal people did not react this way, that her dizziness and her hypervigilance and her inability to articulate the event to anyone—not even to her sister—meant she was going crazy.

To manage the intolerable texture of these days, Talia had developed a pattern of compulsive shopping. Online, mostly, late at night when the anxiety peaked. Clothing, decorative items, things she did not need. The purchases provided a brief, chemical lift—a moment of control, of choosing, of acquiring something that was hers. But the credit card statements accumulated, and the packages arrived to a home already cluttered with items she could barely remember buying. She had spent nearly eight thousand dollars in the past eighteen months. The financial strain added another layer to her conviction that she was failing, that she could not manage even the basics of her own life.

What finally compelled her to seek help was not a single crisis but an accumulation: a date she had nearly missed, a customer who had asked her a simple question and found her unable to respond, the growing awareness that she was becoming someone she no longer recognized. She sat across from the clinician with her hands folded in her lap, her voice quiet but steady, and said, "I need to know if I'm going to get through this, or if I'm already lost."
